summary: Provides guidelines for operators of 6bone routing equipment to follow for efficient and stable routing in that IPv6 test network. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: The 6bone was a practice field for the new Internet. This is a rule sheet for the groundskeepers.

questions: why are link-local prefixes not advertised in bgp
subtitle: The rulebook that kept routing on the 6bone IPv6 testbed stable: which prefixes may be advertised, to whom, and who polices it.

tldr.problem: The 6Bone was a testbed for IPv6, but its backbone had to stay stable, so every operator needed a common set of routing rules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists which special prefixes must never be advertised, requires route aggregation and bans leaking more-specific routes, sets rules for the 6Bone registry, and defines how sites join and how pTLA status is earned and policed.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational best-practice document that obsoletes RFC 2546, and the unit metadata lists RFC 3152 as updating it.

today: RFC 2772 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2546 and is listed as updated by RFC 3152. Its rules describe the 6Bone as it stood in 2000.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The 6Bone is an IPv6 testbed meant to help IPv6 evolve and be deployed. Because its core backbone must stay stable, all operators need a shared set of rules for deploying IPv6 routing equipment. RFC 2772 is a best-practices Informational document aimed at IPv6 entities operating under the 6Bone testbed TLA allocation.

It uses BGP-4 with the Multiprotocol Extensions (RFC 2283), commonly called BGP4+, as the accepted exterior gateway protocol (EGP), and it uses the RFC 2119 key words. It obsoletes RFC 2546.
sections.eli5: A test network still needs rules, or one person's mistake can break it for everybody. This document writes the rules down.

sections.title: Common Rules for Special Prefixes
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC covers address ranges that must be kept out of the backbone routing table. In short:

  • Link-local (FE80::/10) MUST NOT be advertised through an IGP or EGP. A pTLA that finds such routes coming from another pTLA, or from its own downstream, must filter them and fix the problem in a timely way.
  • Site-local (FEC0::/10) MAY be advertised inside a site but MUST NOT cross transit pNLAs, pTLAs or leaf sites. Sites SHOULD filter inbound as well as outbound.
  • Loopback (::1/128) and unspecified (::0/128) MUST NOT be advertised by any routing protocol.
  • Multicast prefixes MUST NOT be advertised by unicast routing protocols. Only global scope multicast MAY cross transit pNLAs and pTLAs.
  • IPv4-compatible (::/96) addresses SHOULD NOT be used or routed. IGPs MAY advertise them, but EGPs MUST NOT send them to transit pNLAs or pTLAs.
  • IPv4-mapped prefixes MAY be advertised by IGPs inside a site, but MUST NOT be advertised by EGPs.

Core pTLA routers MUST be default-free, though pTLAs MAY give a default route to downstream peers. Undefined unicast prefixes outside 2000::/3 MUST NOT be advertised, and RFC 2471 test addresses are named as an example. Inter-site links MUST use global IPv6 addresses at their endpoints, and IPv4-compatible addresses MUST NOT be used for tunnels. Any pTLA MAY announce the 6to4 prefix into global EBGP, provided it has an active 6to4 router sourcing it.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are like private room numbers inside a building. They only make sense in their own room, so you must never put them on the public map.

sections.title: Aggregation and Routing Policy
sections.content:
Border routers talking EGP with other IPv6 sites MUST aggregate routes, and more-specific routes MUST NOT be leaked into or across the 6Bone backbone.

A leaf site or pNLA MUST advertise to an upstream provider only the prefix assigned by that provider. Announcing another provider's prefix, even to work around multihoming, is not acceptable because it breaks the aggregation model. The one exception is a test, and only when all affected parties know and agree, and the test must not affect the 6bone routing table globally. Site border routers MUST NOT advertise prefixes longer than the one allocated by their upstream.

The 6Bone pTLAs MUST NOT advertise prefixes longer than a pTLA delegation (currently /24 or /28) to other pTLAs unless there is a special peering arrangement, and even then must not leak the more-specifics to pTLAs outside it. Peering may be non-commercial and may allow transit, but no pTLA is required to give or receive transit service.

The 6Bone prefix is 3FFE::/16. The RFC notes that registries were starting to assign /35 sub-TLA blocks from 2001::/16, that peering between such new TLAs and 6Bone pTLAs MAY occur, and that most of these rules are expected to apply there too.
sections.eli5: Each neighborhood should only tell the city about its own streets, not every driveway. If everyone shouted every tiny detail, the city map would be a mess.

sections.title: The Registry and Joining the 6Bone
sections.content:
The 6Bone registry is a RIPE-181 database with IPv6 extensions. Each 6Bone leaf site, pNLA and pTLA MUST maintain three objects: IPv6-site (site description), Inet6num (one record per prefix delegation) and Mntner (contact information). The Mntner object MUST refer to a role or person object, which may live in another registry such as ARIN, APNIC or RIPE-NCC.

A new site should connect to a transit pNLA or pTLA in its region, preferably close to its existing IPv4 physical and routing path. It MUST maintain a DNS server for forward and reverse lookups and keep its registry objects up to date. Its upstream provider MUST delegate the reverse zone to the site (or agree to run primary DNS for it) and MUST create the inet6num object for the delegated space.
sections.eli5: Everyone who joins has to sign the guest book with their name, address and contact person, and run their own phone book, so others can find them if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Becoming a pTLA and Enforcement
sections.content:
Holders of a pTLA allocation are expected to provide production-quality backbone service. An applicant needs at least three months of qualifying experience as an end site or pNLA transit, with maintained registry entries, reliable BGP4+ peering from an IPv6-pingable boundary router, maintained DNS entries (AAAA forward and ip6.int reverse), and an IPv6-reachable web server describing its services. It also needs a support staff of at least two people (three preferred), a shared support mailbox, a potential user community, and a commitment to follow current and future 6Bone operational rules. The 6Bone Operations Group judges applications.

That group monitors adherence to the rules. Membership is mandatory for, and limited to, sites connected to the 6Bone, defined by the members of the 6Bone mailing list who represent participating sites.

Participation is voluntary. When a site spots a problem it SHOULD first contact the site's maintainer through the registry, then bring unresolved issues to the Operations Group, and contact the vendor if a product is at fault. If an issue causes major operational problems, backbone sites SHOULD temporarily set filters to restore service. Section 3.1 also notes that repeated failure to filter leaked routes may lead other pTLAs to manually shut down BGP4+ sessions.
sections.eli5: To become a big-league team you need months of good practice, at least two coaches and a shared email. If someone breaks the rules, you talk to them first, and only block them if it gets bad.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC observes that incorrect routing table entries usually make sites unreachable. It expects that aggregating or rejecting routes by these rules will clean up routing tables and make 6Bone routing less sensitive to denial of service attacks that use misleading routes.

Because the 6Bone is a testbed, denial of service or packet disclosure are to be expected. The pTLA from which an attack originated has ultimate responsibility for isolating and fixing it, and every site should introduce new test systems in places where bugs or misconfigurations will do the least harm to others.
sections.eli5: It is a practice field, so bumps and scrapes happen. Still, the team where trouble started has to clean it up, and new toys should be tried in a safe corner.
